title: Ethereum Foundation “dump” is a $6.4m treasury sale, not a crisis
summary: A sale of this size has no meaningful effect on ETH supply or price, coming in at well under 0.1% of daily trading volume. The more relevant support for ETH is around $2,300, where it has been trading, and the broader flow picture: buying from Bitmine is fading, and spot ETF flows matter more than one-off Foundation conversions. A series of larger Foundation sales into weakness would be the scenario that turns this into a genuine supply story. --- Crypto Twitter called it a dump, but the Ethereum Foundation selling $6.4 million of ETH to cover its running costs is a budget line, not a bear signal. Summary: The Ethereum Foundation sold around 2,785 ETH, worth about $6.4 million, for the USDS stablecoin on CoW Swap Social media posts framed the sale as the Foundation dumping ETH The sale equals well under 0.1% of a single day’s ETH trading volume, and less than Bitmine bought last week The Foundation’s treasury policy sets out regular ETH sales to fund operations when cash reserves fall below about 2.5 years of costs It cut its 2026 budget by around 40% and stakes about 70,000 ETH to reduce reliance on sales The Ethereum Foundation sold around 2,785 ETH, worth roughly $6.4 million, according to on-chain tracker Onchain Lens, swapping the tokens for USDS, the dollar stablecoin issued by the Sky ecosystem, through the decentralised exchange CoW Swap. title: Bond market tensions ease but Treasury yields near 5% and France's debt risks keep investors on edge
summary: There is a bit of a welcome relief in global bonds to start the new week, particularly in Europe after Moody's affirmed France's Aa3 credit rating. Meanwhile, Treasury yields have also settled down a fair bit after an extremely volatile period earlier this month. But in looking at where things are right now, there is still plenty of tension lurking beneath the surface. For one, 10-year Treasury yields are still sitting just below the 5% mark for the time being. And over in Europe, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread remains at levels that would have surely been alarming just a few months ago. So while the selling pressure in the bond market has eased for now, the underlying concerns haven't really changed all that much. And as much as that offers some breathing room for broader markets, there are still plenty of reasons to be cautious. The Fed decision tomorrow is one obvious catalyst, even if policymakers are widely expected to leave interst rates unchanged. And beyond that, I'm also keeping a close watch on big tech earnings this week. On the latter, there's a growing concern over whether the enormous spending behind the AI boom can actually justify the returns . And if earnings from the likes of Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon all back that sentiment, we could see a rather nasty bout of volatility kick in again. title: European markets face a quiet calendar today as central banks and big tech earnings loom
summary: European traders will be greeted with a rather bare economic calendar when they get to their desks today, and I reckon that might suit some market players just fine considering what is on the agenda later this week. In terms of data releases, we only have French consumer confidence for October and the ECB's survey on euro area lending for September. Otherwise, markets will largely be left to their own devices as traders wait on the central bank bonanza to roll into town . Wall Street at least provided a more positive lead in overnight trading, with the S&P 500 posting 0.7% gains and the Nasdaq closing 0.8% higher. Tech stocks helped to drive the rebound but caution is very much still up in the air, especially with the recent volatility surrounding the AI trade. As for geopolitical tensions, we are seeing more of the same old, same old. Fresh diplomatic efforts involving Iran are offering some hope of de-escalation but continued attacks on Saudi Arabia are keeping oil supply risks firmly in the picture. As such, I wouldn't be surprised if we see traders take on a more reserved and cautious approach to trading today. After all, the focus now turns to the BOC and Fed decisions tomorrow, followed by the ECB on Thursday and BOJ on Friday. And that is without mentioning big tech earnings with Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon all set to put the AI spending debate back under the spotlight. title: Japan September services PPI holds at 3.7% y/y, in line with forecast, before BoJ
summary: An in-line print is unlikely to move the yen much on its own, but it removes one possible dovish surprise before Friday’s decision and keeps the backdrop supportive of December hike pricing. Steady services inflation strengthens the case for the Outlook Report to effectively declare underlying inflation has reached 2%, which would support the yen and short-end JGB yields. The bigger moves are still likely to come from the BoJ’s vote split, Ueda’s press conference and Wednesday’s Fed decision. title: Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA’s 0.8% forecast
summary: The Australian dollar and front-end yields are set up for a binary reaction. With implied hike odds already above half, a trimmed mean at or above 1.0% would push November pricing closer to fully priced and support the currency. A 0.9% or lower print could see that pricing unwind quickly. Oil is central to the headline story: the fuel spike reflects the global energy shock tied to the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would keep headline inflation elevated into year-end. The services component matters most for the RBA, since broadening price pressure would undercut the argument that this is purely an imported energy shock. The release coincides with RBA officials appearing before Senate Estimates, adding to the event risk. --- Earlier: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac’s Ellis says read the data calls --- Australia’s core inflation is set to overshoot the RBA’s own forecast for another quarter, and with the banks split down the middle, Wednesday’s print may decide whether the Board hikes on Melbourne Cup Day. title: Goldman Sachs: AI buildout to add up to 50bp to US core PCE, but the boost is temporary
summary: The analysis adds a structural layer to an inflation backdrop already strained by energy, which argues against easing and supports the case for central banks on tightening paths, including the Fed and the Bank of Japan, to keep a hawkish bias into 2027. Japan’s projected 0.3 point boost is notable ahead of this week’s BoJ meeting, where the key question is whether underlying inflation has reached 2%. For bonds, a temporary but well-timed price shock could keep front-end yields supported. For equities, the finding that AI lifts prices more than growth outside Asian supply hubs feeds into investor scrutiny of returns on AI spending. Oil remains the bigger swing factor, but AI now adds to the pressure from the goods side. --- Speaking of inflation, coming today: Japan services PPI preview: 3.7% pace in focus ahead of Friday’s BoJ decision --- AI is showing up in inflation faster than in growth, and Goldman Sachs reckons the price bump will be temporary, though not before central banks have to sit through it.
